To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following cancer therapies cause heart failure in humans, and in animal models, through distinct molecular mechanisms, and that understanding these mechanisms will allow us to develop new strategies to prevent heart failure in cancer patients.

1) Anthracycline antibiotics cause cardiomyocyte death by a combination of apoptosis and necrosis, and 2) Tyrosine kinase inhibitors cause cardiomyocyte apoptosis by activation of a novel signaling pathway involving the protein kinase mTOR.
the molecular mechanisms of cardiac damage caused by anticancer therapies can be used to develop new therapies to prevent or ameliorate the effects of these therapies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms underlying cancer therapies-induced cardiotoxicity and developing novel strategies to prevent or reverse these side effects.
the mechanisms of cardiac dysfunction induced by cancer therapies, and the development of new therapies for the prevention of this complication.
the molecular basis of the cardiac toxicity of cancer therapies, and the development of new therapies to prevent or treat these side effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cardiovascular side effects of cancer therapies are a major problem in cancer therapy and that the mechanisms of these effects are being rapidly elucidated.

cancer therapy is associated with heart failure and that there is a great need for further research into the mechanisms of cardiac injury by cancer therapy, and the development of new strategies to reduce or prevent cardiac injury by cancer treatment

there is a need to develop better therapies for cancer and that these therapies should be evaluated in preclinical models for cardiac side effects, and that the mechanisms for cardiac side effects should be studied and understood so that these side effects may be prevented or treated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel model to study the effects of anthracycline cardiotoxicity and that we are beginning to elucidate the molecular mechanisms that lead to this toxicity.

cancer therapies can cause heart failure, but that the molecular and cellular mechanisms are different from those causing heart failure in patients with hypertension, coronary heart disease and diabetes, suggesting that new therapies will be needed to treat cancer patients with cardiac complications of anticancer therapies.
the heart is not just a pump but is also a target for many anticancer therapies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the heart is not a static organ.
there is a need for a paradigm shift in the way we view cancer therapy-associated cardiotoxicity.
the mechanisms of cardiac injury and dysfunction from cancer therapies are not the same as those from other causes of heart failure.
